passage.title: The Mold That Changed Medicine
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Before 1940, a tiny scratch from a rose thorn or a scraped knee could turn into a deadly illness. Doctors had no drug that could kill bad germs in the blood without hurting good cells too. In the fall of 1928, a Scottish doctor named Alexander Fleming came back to his London lab after a trip. Before leaving, he had stacked several glass dishes of bacteria on a corner bench. As he checked the pile, one open dish caught his eye. A stray speck of mold had drifted in through the air and contaminated the gel.

Most lab workers would have tossed the spoiled glass dish straight into the wash bin. Fleming, though, stopped to look closely at the strange pattern on the plate. Around the pale green patch of mold, the thick colonies of harmful germs had been completely dissolved by a clear ring of liquid. Something oozing from the green bread mold was stopping the bad germs from growing. Fleming named this active mold juice penicillin.

Fleming knew the mold juice was potent against germs, yet he could not turn it into a lasting drug on his own. The raw liquid was extremely fragile and lost its germ-fighting power within days. For ten years, Fleming tried to pull the pure healing stuff out of the thin broth. Each time, he failed. At last, he printed his notes in a book and hoped that skilled chemists might solve the puzzle.

In 1938, a team at Oxford led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain read Fleming's notes and took up the task. Working day and night with giant milk churns, bath trays, and clay bedpans, they grew gallons of the green mold. Chain found a way to freeze-dry the broth so the delicate medicine could be extracted as a stable brown powder without losing its strength. When they gave the powder to sick mice in 1940, the mice got well fast.

By 1943, big plants in the United States were using deep vats and corn water to brew the drug. Soon they made enough of the powder to save thousands of hurt troops. What began as an accidental speck of mold on a messy lab bench became a life-saving drug only after a second team figured out how to purify and store it.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"Around the pale green patch of mold, the thick colonies of harmful germs had been completely dissolved by a clear ring of liquid."

In this sentence, what actually dissolved the colonies of harmful germs?

options.text: The thick colonies of harmful germs
A sharp rose thorn placed on the glass plate
Hot soap and water from the laboratory wash bin
A clear ring of liquid oozing from the mold

questions.provingSentenceText: Around the pale green patch of mold, the thick colonies of harmful germs had been completely dissolved by a clear ring of liquid.
questions.childTip: Look after the passive verb 'had been completely dissolved by' to find what wiped out the germs.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive-voice sentence, 'the thick colonies of harmful germs' is the receiver of the action. The true actor performing 'had been dissolved' comes after 'by': 'a clear ring of liquid' (Option B).

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"Chain found a way to freeze-dry the broth so the delicate medicine could be extracted as a stable brown powder without losing its strength."

What does the word "extracted" mean as it is used in this sentence?

options.text: Hidden inside a locked medical journal for ten years
Thrown away into a laboratory trash can
Pulled out and separated from a liquid mixture
Mixed with harmful germs to make the bacteria grow faster

questions.provingSentenceText: Chain found a way to freeze-dry the broth so the delicate medicine could be extracted as a stable brown powder without losing its strength.
questions.childTip: Connect 'extracted' to Fleming's goal in Paragraph 3: to pull the pure healing stuff out of the thin broth.
questions.parentExplanation: The Latin root 'ex- + trahere' means to draw out. In context, Chain freeze-dried the liquid broth so the pure medicine could be drawn out and separated as a stable brown powder (Option A).

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 3, why was Alexander Fleming unable to treat patients with penicillin right after he discovered it in 1928?

options.text: He accidentally threw the glass dish into the wash bin before naming the mold.
The raw mold liquid was unstable and lost its germ-fighting power within a few days.
Hospitals in London refused to use any medicine discovered during a summer trip.
The green mold only dissolved healthy human cells and left harmful germs alone.

questions.provingSentenceText: The raw liquid was extremely fragile and lost its germ-fighting power within days.
questions.childTip: Click the sentence in Paragraph 3 that explains what happened to the raw liquid within days.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 explains that although Fleming knew the mold juice was potent, 'The raw liquid was extremely fragile and lost its germ-fighting power within days,' preventing him from turning it into a usable drug on his own (Option A).

questions.prompt: Which evidence does the author provide in Paragraph 4 to support the claim that turning penicillin into a usable drug required clever chemistry?

options.text: Ernst Chain freeze-dried the mold broth to extract a stable brown powder that cured sick mice.
Fleming left several glass dishes of bacteria stacked on a corner bench in London.
A tiny scratch from a rose thorn could cause a dangerous illness before 1940.
Most researchers tossed spoiled glass dishes straight into the laboratory wash bin.

questions.provingSentenceText: Chain found a way to freeze-dry the broth so the delicate medicine could be extracted as a stable brown powder without losing its strength.
questions.childTip: Look in Paragraph 4 for the breakthrough that solved the problem of the fragile liquid losing its strength.
questions.parentExplanation: Aligned to ELAGSE5RI8, the author proves the importance of chemical purification by showing how Ernst Chain freeze-dried the broth into a stable brown powder that kept its strength and cured sick mice (Option B).

questions.prompt: PART A: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?

options.text: Scientists should always leave their laboratory windows open during summer vacation so mold can grow.
Penicillin became a life-saving medicine because Fleming noticed an accidental mold spore and later scientists found a way to purify it.
Milk churns and clay bedpans are better for growing bacteria than glass dishes.
Howard Florey and Ernst Chain proved that Alexander Fleming's 1928 notes were completely wrong.

questions.provingSentenceText: What began as an accidental speck of mold on a messy lab bench became a life-saving drug only after a second team figured out how to purify and store it.
questions.childTip: Look at the final sentence of Paragraph 5, which connects Fleming's discovery to Florey and Chain's work.
questions.parentExplanation: The passage traces how two stages of scientific work—Fleming's sharp observation in 1928 and Florey and Chain's purification ten years later—combined to create usable penicillin (Option A).

"Before leaving, he had stacked several glass dishes of bacteria on a corner bench."
"Working day and night with giant milk churns, bath trays, and clay bedpans, they grew gallons of the green mold."
"What began as an accidental speck of mold on a messy lab bench became a life-saving drug only after a second team figured out how to purify and store it."

questions.provingSentenceText: What began as an accidental speck of mold on a messy lab bench became a life-saving drug only after a second team figured out how to purify and store it.
questions.childTip: Pick the quote that ties together both the accidental mold discovery and the second team's purification work.
questions.parentExplanation: Option D directly proves the central idea in Part A by summarizing how both Fleming's observation and the Oxford team's purification were essential to creating penicillin.
